fortuitous

for-TOO-ih-tus -- from Latin fors ('chance'). Despite the resemblance, it is not related to fort or fortitude, which come from a different Latin root, fortis, meaning 'strong.' · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Fortuitous is happening by lucky chance rather than by design.

The two researchers' fortuitous meeting at a conference coffee cart led to a breakthrough neither could have found working alone.

Example

It was entirely fortuitous that the hikers stumbled on the abandoned cabin just as the storm broke -- they hadn't even known it was there.

The hikers never planned or expected to find shelter -- that lucky, unplanned timing is exactly what makes something fortuitous.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

accidental: Accidental means nobody intended it -- a spilled drink, a wrong turn -- and it says nothing about luck at all; accidents are usually unwelcome. Fortuitous also means unplanned, but it frames the chance event as a stroke of fortune, something that simply fell into place.

serendipitous: Serendipitous chance hands you a delightful discovery you weren't even looking for -- a cure found while studying something else. Fortuitous is broader: any event that happens by chance rather than design. Every serendipitous find is fortuitous, but a fortuitous event needn't discover anything.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

planned: deliberately arranged ahead of time

inevitable: certain to happen no matter what

Where it sits · how much pure luck is involved — fortunate → fortuitous → providential

fortunate vs. fortuitous: Fortunate is weaker than fortuitous: finding a parking spot out front is merely fortunate, while a fortuitous find carries a sharper sense of pure chance delivering exactly what you needed.

providential vs. fortuitous: Providential goes further than fortuitous: a fortuitous arrival is a happy accident, but reaching the shelter minutes before the storm feels providential — luck so extreme it seems heaven-sent.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — fort-/fortu-

root — fort-/fortu-: chance (Latin (fors))

Put it together

Put it together: Fortuitous comes from the Latin noun fors, meaning 'chance' -- so something fortuitous happens purely by chance, not through effort or design. (It only looks like fort or fortitude, which actually come from a different Latin root, fortis, meaning 'strong.')

Use the root in a new word: fortune

Use the root in a new word: fortune: Grandpa always said the family's fortune turned the year the orchard finally bloomed.

Root Check

Word Choice

Fortuitous describes something that happens by pure chance -- it doesn't, by itself, say whether the chance event was good or bad, though in everyday use people almost always mean a lucky accident.
